definition: A Wi-Fi feature that cryptographically protects management frames, such as deauthentication and disassociation messages, so an outsider cannot forge or replay them. It is required in WPA3.
example: An attacker sends forged deauthentication frames to kick laptops off the office Wi-Fi, but with PMF required the laptops ignore the unsigned frames and stay connected.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
keyPoints: Stops forged disconnect (deauth) attacks used for denial of service and to push clients toward an evil twin
Protects the frames against forgery; it does not hide their contents
Mandatory for WPA3 and for new Wi-Fi certified devices
Needs a WPA2 or WPA3 network with a key or 802.1X; it cannot protect an open network
Can be set to optional so older clients without it can still join

definition: A purge sanitization method for media whose data is already encrypted: the encryption keys are destroyed, so the remaining ciphertext can no longer be decrypted.
example: Before returning leased laptops with self-encrypting SSDs, IT runs the drives' cryptographic erase command, which wipes the internal key in seconds and leaves the stored data unreadable.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
keyPoints: Counts as purge under NIST SP 800-88
Only works if all the data was encrypted from the start and every copy of the key is destroyed
Fast: seconds instead of hours of overwriting
Often the only practical purge for cloud and virtual storage
Degaussing does nothing to SSDs; overwriting SSDs is unreliable; cryptographic erase avoids both problems

definition: A credentialed scan logs in to each host with an account and reads its software, patches and settings directly. A non-credentialed scan works only from the network, guessing from open ports and service banners what an outside attacker would see.
example: A non-credentialed scan reports a server only as running SSH on port 22; the credentialed scan of the same server lists 40 missing operating system patches and a vulnerable library inside an application.
keyPoints: Credentialed: deeper and more accurate, fewer false positives
Non-credentialed: the attacker's outside view, finds exposed services and network weaknesses
Credentialed scans need a protected scanning account, ideally limited to what the scan requires
Confirm the login worked on each host, or a clean report may mean nothing was checked
Mature programs run both

term: Encrypted DNS (DoH and DoT) as a blind spot
definition: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt name lookups. When a browser, app or malware sends them to an outside resolver, the lookups skip the company's DNS server, so DNS filtering and DNS logging never see them.
example: Malware queries its control domain through a public DoH service over port 443; the company's DNS filter and SIEM show nothing because the request looked like ordinary web traffic.
keyPoints: DoH uses port 443, mixing with normal web traffic; DoT uses port 853
Fix: send all DNS, encrypted or not, only to the enterprise resolver
Block known outside DoH resolvers and port 853, and disable or point browser DoH settings to the internal resolver
The enterprise resolver itself can offer encrypted DNS
Good for privacy at home, a monitoring gap in a company if unmanaged
